# Learn the idea, verify the detail {#sec-learning}

Qt rewards a clear mental model and current references. Know why bindings, event loops, and
ownership work. Look up exact APIs every time.

## Read from primary sources {#sec-reading}

Start with the Qt module overview, then a current example, then the reference for the types it
uses. Tests in Qt and this template show supported behaviour better than old snippets online.

## Spot old Qt advice {#sec-stale-qt}

Qt 5 code often still compiles, but it can teach the wrong shape. Prefer CMake,
`qt_add_qml_module()`, typed signal connections, `QML_ELEMENT`, and required properties
over qmake, string-based connections, manual type registration, and context properties.

| Older Qt advice | Current Qt Quick approach |
|---|---|
| qmake and `.pro` files | CMake and `qt_add_qml_module()` |
| `qmlRegisterType()` in `main()` | declarative QML type registration |
| context properties | typed required properties |
| string-based `SIGNAL` and `SLOT` | typed function-pointer connections |
| `import QtQuick 2.15` | versionless `import QtQuick` |

Older examples can still explain a concept, but verify the APIs against the Qt version your
application uses before adopting the code.

## Give an agent ground truth {#sec-agent-skills}

Project rules belong in `AGENTS.md`. Current Qt documentation and Qt-specific agent skills
supply the missing API context. Tests, compiler warnings, `qmllint`, and sanitizers decide
whether a suggested change works.

The Qt agent-skills repository offers focused guidance for QML, CMake, tests, and review, as
well as a documentation server for looking up APIs. They provide framework context; your
project's `AGENTS.md` supplies local commands and architecture rules. The same tests and checks
help a person and an agent find mistakes early.

## Keep ownership of the result {#sec-own}

Read generated code, run the checks, and keep only what you can explain. An assistant can
accelerate work. It cannot own the release.
